# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.” 
 You can find the discussion draft text here . 
 You can find the section-by-section summary of the discussion draft here . 
 You can read Congressman Obernolte’s and Congresswoman Trahan’s op-ed here .

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 (GAAIA), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence (AI) at the federal level. 

 The draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.

 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.

 Objectives of the GAAIA 

 The 269-page draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”

 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 

 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.

 Frontier AI Framework: The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations: The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements: Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 

 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.

 Codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation 

 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include:

 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 “This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards,” the document said.

 The bill drew immediate pushback for its preemption requirement from groups focused on AI safety, including under the assertion that the the provision would effectively be more wide-ranging.

 Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation and a former Democratic representative from Oklahoma, said preemption of state laws would be a “generational mistake.”

 “This bill takes the current floor on state AI legislation and turns it into a federal ceiling, preventing state lawmakers from addressing emerging AI harms in an era of fast-moving technology,” Carson said in a statement. “Over the past two decades, state lawmakers have proven to be a backstop for tech accountability, fighting for families and communities even as Congress has stalled on creating guardrails.”

 Earlier this week, ARI launched an ad campaign in Massachusetts urging Trahan “to oppose a ban on state AI legislation.”

 Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the safety-focused Alliance for Secure AI, praised the bill’s bipartisanship and its focus on catastrophic risk and loss of control, but opposed the preemption requirement.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

 Mandates

 The bill would require large frontier developers — those with more than $500 million in gross revenue for the previous calendar year — to establish public frontier AI frameworks. The frameworks would include information on whether a model could pose a “catastrophic risk,” defined by the bill as “a foreseeable and material risk” of death or injury of more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and the thresholds the developer used to determine that risk.

 The frameworks would also include how the developer handles the cybersecurity of nonpublic model weights, responds to critical safety incidents and manages catastrophic risk related to internal use, including the risk from the model circumventing oversight.

 Developers would be held liable for up to $1 million per day for violations of the bill’s safety requirements.

 Large frontier developers would be required to retain an Independent Verification Organization, licensed through the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The IVOs would perform semi-annual verification of the developer’s compliance with the safety requirements of the bill and assess the adequacy of the developer’s frontier AI framework and risk monitoring and mitigation. The results of the audit would then be submitted to CAISI.

 Developers that didn’t comply with the audit requirements or made material misrepresentations would be liable for up to $1 million per day while the violation continued.

 Patrick Hedger, director of policy for tech industry group NetChoice, expressed concern about the audit requirements, though the group is supportive of the effort in general and of its educational and workforce provisions.

 Unpacking the Great American AI Act
 Key provisions on AI transparency, audits, and federal preemption Written by : Tony Samp Danny Tobey Ashley Carr Alicia Smith Michael Atleson On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence (AI) legislation titled the “Great American AI Act” (GAAIA). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint op-ed in Bloomberg Law .

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and preemption: “Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough.”

 AI’s impact on the workforce: “Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.”

 US leadership internationally: “By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.”

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I)

 Workforce (Title II)

 Cybersecurity (Title III)

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV)

 Transparency in frontier AI models 

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (Section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (Section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (Section 113).

 Section 111 

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a “frontier AI framework” focused on risk mitigation and the handling of “catastrophic risk.” All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any “critical safety incidents” to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation (CAISI).

 Section 112 

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee “independent verification organizations (IVOs)” that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform “audits and assessments.”

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s “frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks.”

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General (AG) and state AGs. Such referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both Sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113 

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding “AI violations.” This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations “related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence.”

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills 

 All three sections borrow heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is thus the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another recently enacted state law in Virginia focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable preemption provisions 

 Title I of the bill would preempt state laws and rules “specifically regulating the development of” any AI model, where “development” is broadly defined as “acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment.” The bill explains that the purpose of such preemption is to allow the federal government to “establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks.” Such preemption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or preempt state laws or rules of "general applicability." Thus, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating companion bots  and commercial chatbot interactions .

 However, the preemption language could preempt several state laws imposing obligations on developers, including the three frontier developer laws described above.

 GAAIA incorporates multiple bipartisan bills 

 The draft text incorporates provisions from several bipartisan bills on AI policy addressing a variety of issues, including cybersecurity, AI education and workforce, fraud deterrence, whistleblower protections, data center energy efficiencies, and others.

 The draft bill would formally codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation in the Commerce Department, with $100 million per year authorized for fiscal 2027-2029. October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, and for inviting the public to comment before introduction. We are submitting these comments to that end.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members come to this from different places - school board meetings, shop floors, church basements, research labs - but we share one conviction: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions (Sections 102, 111 and 112) with a frontier moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, paired with a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified, open-weight models included. We set out our full request, section by section, below.

## What the draft gets right

We want to start with what we would keep, because it matters.

The draft names the danger honestly. Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures, and "loss of control" of a model. Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of mass casualties or more than $1 billion in property damage. Very few federal bills have been willing to write those words down. You have, and we thank you.

The draft also borrows the strongest tools the states have built. Sections 111 through 113 track, in large part, California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (in effect since January 1, 2026), New York's RAISE Act as amended and signed on March 27, 2026 (effective January 1, 2027), and Illinois' frontier safety law. The whistleblower protections in Section 113 are real protections: they cannot be waived by contract, including by pre-dispute arbitration agreements. We support Section 113 without qualification. We also support the Section 311 grants to maintainers of critical open-source software and the federal testbed program in Section 401.

So the question is not whether you see the problem. The question is whether the draft's tools are equal to the problem the draft itself describes. They are not.

## A report is a receipt, not a brake

Section 111(g) requires a frontier developer that discovers a critical safety incident to report it to the CAISI Director within 15 days - within 24 hours to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Consider what that sentence assumes. It assumes the incident will have already happened. A regime built on a 15-day reporting clock is a regime for documenting catastrophes, not preventing them.

The draft's own definitions make our case for us. If losing control of a frontier model is a live enough possibility to be listed as a reportable event in Section 101, then it is a live enough possibility to prevent. A law that treats "loss of control" as paperwork has conceded the argument. We ask you to follow your own definitions to their conclusion: if these systems can be lost, they should not be built until we know how to hold them.

## Audits of a company's own plan cannot protect the public

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization to audit them at least semi-annually. This is better than nothing. But look at what the auditor is auditing.

The "frontier AI framework" being verified is written by the developer (Section 111(a)). The risk thresholds are set by the developer. The standard the audit measures against - "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" (Section 101) - is defined by weighing the model's anticipated benefits against its catastrophic risks, a judgment the company makes about its own product. An audit can confirm that a laboratory followed its own plan. It cannot confirm that the plan protects anyone outside the laboratory. Most importantly, no audit can show that a frontier system is controllable, because no developer on earth can show that today. An audit regime that cannot certify control, and does not require it, will tell the public a great deal about process and nothing about safety.

We would replace this with what the word "verification" actually promises: independent certification that a frontier model is reliably controllable as the legal condition of training and serving it - that is, the enforcement mechanism of the pause we describe below.

## The federal floor expires; the state laws you would freeze do not

Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment. Section 121 preempts state and local laws specifically regulating the development of AI models for the same three years. Put those two facts together and the trade becomes clear. Congress would freeze California's, New York's and Illinois' frontier-development obligations - laws that are already in force or already enacted and effective January 1, 2027, and that do not expire - in exchange for federal requirements that lapse around 2029 unless reauthorized. If Congress does not act on schedule, the country is left with no binding frontier-development rules at all, and states would have to start over.

Your own op-ed puts it better than we can: "Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough." We agree. Protections that depend on a sunset clause are not enough either.

Congress has already weighed in on this question. On July 1, 2025, the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strike a ten-year ban on state AI laws from the reconciliation bill. Since then, the December 2025 executive order created a Department of Justice task force to challenge state AI laws in court, and the March 20, 2026 White House framework urged Congress to preempt state laws that impose "undue burdens." The states are not the obstacle to safety here. They are the only governments that have acted. We ask you to strike Section 121 and let them keep acting.

Our members are watching this closely. In our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters, 63 percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

## The draft does nothing about what is already deployed - especially open weights

Section 111(c) requires a transparency report before or concurrent with deploying a frontier model. That report is a document on a website. It constrains nothing after release.

For models served by a single company, the operator can at least be identified and ordered to act. Open-weight models are different, and they are the fastest-growing part of the frontier. Frontier-class open weights are already published and downloadable by anyone, anywhere: Meta's Llama family, and from Chinese developers DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen. Once weights are public, there is no recall, no patch everyone must take, no way to reach every copy. US cloud providers host and serve them today.

The draft's answer to this is Section 321, a report on model weight, data center and open-source security. We do not need another report to tell us that published weights stay published. We need a wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified should be withdrawn within 12 months, open-weight models included, and US cloud providers should be required to stop hosting and serving them. That is the only intervention that matches the facts of an open release.

## Penalties that cannot deter, aimed at companies rather than people

The draft backs its requirements with civil penalties - reported at up to $1 million per day while a violation continues, enforced through referrals to the Attorney General and state attorneys general. A company spending tens of billions of dollars a year on training compute will book that as a cost of doing business. And the penalties run against corporate entities, not against the people who make the decision to train or to serve a frontier model.

We ask for criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the Act. Two-thirds of voters in our August 2026 survey (66 percent) said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm.

## The industry is asking for what we are asking for

On June 4, 2026 - the same day you released this draft - Anthropic wrote that "it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier AI development, warning that recursive self-improvement might increase the risk of humans losing control of AI systems. A frontier developer, in public, asked for the option of a pause.

We agree with Anthropic about the danger. But an option is not a policy. A voluntary, coordinated pause will be broken by the first laboratory that sees an advantage in breaking it, which is precisely what Anthropic warns about. What the industry says it wants only works if it is binding, statutory and enforced. That is the job in front of you.

## What we ask

1. **A pause on frontier training.** Add a new section to Title I imposing an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP, until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Use the draft's own threshold: Section 101 already defines a frontier model by the 10^26 FLOP line. We are not asking you to identify new systems to regulate. We are asking you to stop training the ones you have already defined.

2. **A wind-down of deployed frontier models.** Within 12 months, withdraw any deployed frontier model that cannot be independently certified as controllable, including open-weight models already released - Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Qwen - and require US cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them.

3. **Criminal liability for executives.** Criminal penalties for any executive who knowingly trains or serves a frontier model in violation of the Act. Keep the civil penalties as a floor, and extend Section 113's whistleblower protections to workers who refuse to take part in a prohibited training or serving arrangement.

4. **Strike Section 121.** No preemption of state AI safety laws - not for three years, not for one. 63 percent of voters in our August 2026 survey oppose blocking states, and 74 percent want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release.

5. **Keep CAISI, but give it the mission that matters.** We support the $100 million annual authorization in Section 102 only as part of this moratorium. Repurpose CAISI as the enforcement body for the pause: run the independent certification of controllability, verify the wind-down, monitor compute at the training-run level, and refer violations for prosecution. A standards center that issues voluntary guidelines and licenses auditors cannot stop a race. An enforcement body with a stop order can.

A pause above the 10^26 FLOP line leaves nearly all of AI untouched - the tools our members use at work, in classrooms, in hospitals, in research. It is not a pause on artificial intelligence. It is a pause on the small number of training runs that no one can currently control.

We recognize this is a significant rewrite. But you have written a bill that defines "loss of control" as a reportable incident, and then schedules the report for 15 days later. The honest response to your own findings is not better documentation of the loss of control. It is preventing it. There is no safe path on the current trajectory, and 49 percent of voters in our survey support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems, with only 31 percent opposed. We would welcome a meeting with both offices before introduction, and we can bring researchers and members from your districts who can speak to this directly.

Thank you for your consideration, and for the seriousness with which you have approached this issue.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

cc: Rep. Scott Franklin, Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, Rep. Erin Houchin, Rep. Scott Peters; House Committee on Energy and Commerce

## No safe path on the current trajectory: pause frontier training now

**Our position on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) discussion draft (Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, June 4, 2026): oppose as drafted. The reporting and audit provisions in Sections 102, 111 and 112 should be replaced with a frontier moratorium.**

**Who we are.** FRC is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members are not anti-technology. We are against building systems no one can control.

**The problem in one paragraph.** The draft's own definitions concede the danger: Section 101 lists "loss of control" of a frontier model as a "critical safety incident," and then Section 111 gives the developer 15 days to report it. # FRONTIER RESTRAINT COALITION - E&C one-pager

## No safe path on the current trajectory: pause frontier training now

**On the Great American AI Act discussion draft (Obernolte-Trahan, June 4, 2026): we oppose as drafted. Replace Secs. 102, 111 and 112 with a frontier moratorium.**

**Who we are.** A national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers - not anti-technology, against building systems no one can control.

**The problem.** Section 101 calls "loss of control" of a frontier model a reportable "critical safety incident"; Section 111 gives the developer 15 days to report it. Paperwork for a catastrophe does not prevent one. No developer can show its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable. Reporting does not stop the race.

## Five asks

1. **Pause frontier training.** Immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP - the draft's own threshold (Sec. 101) - until Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled.
2. **Wind down deployed frontier models.** Within 12 months, withdraw any deployed frontier model that cannot be independently certified - open-weight models included (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen). US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
3. **Hold executives personally liable.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the Act.
4. **Strike Sec. 121 (preemption).** Don't freeze California's and New York's frontier laws - in force or enacted, with no expiry date - for federal rules that sunset in three years. The Senate rejected a state AI-law ban 99-1 on July 1, 2025.
5. **Repurpose CAISI (Sec. 102).** Keep the $100 million a year, but as the pause's enforcement body: certify controllability, verify the wind-down, monitor training compute, refer violations for prosecution.

**What we are not asking for.** A pause above the 10^26 FLOP line leaves nearly all AI untouched - the tools used in classrooms, hospitals and workplaces. This is not a pause on AI; it is a pause on the handful of training runs nobody can control. We support Sec. 113 whistleblower protections, Sec. 311 open-source security grants and Sec. 401 testbeds as written.

**Even industry asks for this.** The day the draft dropped, Anthropic said it "would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier AI development. An option is not a policy. Only a binding pause holds.

**The politics (FRC survey, Aug 2026, n=1,512 registered voters).** 74% want companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. 63% say federal law should not block state AI safety laws. 66% back criminal penalties for AI-caused mass harm. 49% support a temporary halt; 31% oppose.

**Contact:** Daniel Osei, Policy Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition.

{"content": "# FRC - Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft: asks by section

Board-approved positions (messaging guide v4, 30 Sep 2026). Section numbers and provision descriptions checked against the sponsors' section-by-section summary and the discussion draft text (released 4 Jun 2026).

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **New provision - not in the draft.** Frontier moratorium | **Request.** This is FRC's core ask | Add a new Title I section: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled | No safe path on the current trajectory - a race no one can stop is the danger, not the answer. |
| **Sec. 101 - Definitions** (frontier model = trained above 10^26 operations; "critical safety incident" includes "loss of control"; "catastrophic risk" = mass casualties / $1B+ damage) | Keep the threshold; act on the words | Keep the 10^26 FLOP frontier threshold and apply it as the pause line; use the definitions to define what the moratorium covers | The draft names "loss of control" as a reportable incident - if it can happen, training above that line should stop first. |
| **Sec. 102 - Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI)** (voluntary guidelines; system evaluation; $100M/yr FY2027-2029; licenses IVOs) | Support **only** as the moratorium's enforcement body | Rewrite CAISI's mission: run independent certification of controllability, verify the wind-down, monitor training compute, refer violations for prosecution - keep the $100M/yr for that job | Voluntary guidelines and auditor licensing cannot stop a race; an enforcement body with a stop order can. |
| **Sec. 111 - Transparency in Frontier AI** (frontier AI framework; pre-deployment transparency report; 15-day critical safety incident reports, 24 hours to law enforcement if imminent risk) | Oppose as a substitute for prevention; keep incident reporting as an interim measure | Replace the framework-and-report regime with the training pause; retain the incident-reporting mechanism until the pause is in force | A report is a receipt - a 15-day clock starts after the "loss of control" it describes. |
| **Sec. 112 - Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs)** (semi-annual audits of large frontier developers; referrals to AGs; civil penalties) | Oppose as drafted | Replace audits of a developer's own framework with independent certification of controllability as the legal condition of training or serving a frontier model; add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate | An audit can show a lab followed its own plan; only certification can show the public is safe. |
| **Sec. 113 - Whistleblower protections** (non-waivable, incl. arbitration contracts) | Support | Keep as drafted; extend protections to workers who refuse to take part in a prohibited training or serving arrangement | The people closest to the risk need the strongest protection. |
| **Sec. 121 - Federalization of state laws regulating AI model development** (preempts state laws targeting development; 3-year sunset) | Oppose - strike | Strike the section entirely; preserve California SB 53 (in effect 1 Jan 2026), the New York RAISE Act (effective 1 Jan 2027), Illinois' law, and other states' authority to act | Don't trade state laws that don't expire for federal rules that sunset in three years. |
| **Sec. 122 - GAO review of federal AI adoption** | Support; outside our core remit | No change requested | Oversight of government use of AI is worthwhile. |
| **Secs. 131-132 - Financial crimes using AI; AI impersonation of federal officials** | Support; outside our core remit | No change requested | Real harms with real penalties - worth keeping regardless of the frontier question. |
| **Sec. 311 - CISA grants for critical open-source software maintainers** | Support | Keep, but do not treat it as a frontier-weights measure | Software security is worth funding; it does nothing about published model weights. |
| **Sec. 321 - Report on model weight, data center and open-source security** | Oppose as a response to released weights | Replace with the wind-down: withdraw deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified within 12 months, open-weight models included (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen); require US cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them | A report cannot un-publish weights - only a wind-down limits what is already in the wild. |
| **Sec. 401 / Title IV - AI testbeds, NAIRR, international standards** | Support with a change | Keep the testbeds and NAIRR; require testbeds to serve control and certification research, not capability scaling; direct the international standards work toward a multilateral pause | The question is controllability, not more capability. |

*FRC also asks that criminal penalties apply to executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the Act (see moratorium row above). Full argument in comment_letter_GAAIA.md.*

**Sources checked:** sponsors' press release and section-by-section summary (obernolte.house.gov, trahan.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026); draft text table of contents; Roll Call, FedScoop and Axios coverage (4 Jun 2026); ArentFox Schiff and DLA Piper analyses (Jun 2026); California SB 53 text (leginfo); Governor Hochul's release on the RAISE chapter amendment (27 Mar 2026).

**What we told Congress about the new AI bill**

Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan have released a draft federal AI bill, the Great American AI Act, and asked for public comments. FRC filed ours this week.

**What we told Congress about the new AI bill**

Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan have released a draft federal AI bill, the Great American AI Act, and asked for public comments. FRC filed ours this week.

The draft would require big AI labs to publish safety plans, report serious incidents within 15 days, and get audited. It would also block state AI safety laws, including California's and New York's, for three years.

We said no. Reporting a disaster is not preventing one. We asked Congress to pause training of any model above 10^26 FLOP until it certifies these systems can be reliably controlled; to wind down deployed frontier models that can't be independently certified within 12 months, open-weight models included; and to hold executives criminally liable. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

Want to add your voice? Email your comment to GAAIA@mail.house.gov. Every message counts.

---

Count: let me count later. Target ~150 (say 130-170).

Then staff_qa.md — 4 answers ≤120 words each.

Q1 (Majority E&C staff): The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
A: Because everything in the draft happens after the fact, or on the developer's own terms. Section 101 defines "loss of control" as a critical safety incident; Section 111 gives the developer 15 days to report it. That's a receipt for a catastrophe, not a prevention. CAISI as drafted issues voluntary guidelines and licenses auditors; the audits measure a company against a framework the company wrote itself, judged against an "acceptable level" of catastrophic risk that the company sets. No audit can show a frontier model is controllable, because no developer can show that today. What's missing is the one tool that prevents: a pause on training above 10^26 FLOP - the draft's own threshold - until Congress certifies control, plus a wind-down of models already deployed that can't be certified.

Word count ~130. Need ≤120. Trim.

Q2 (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned): Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
A: Dropping Section 121 would remove one fatal flaw, and we'd work with the sponsors on it - 63% of voters say federal law shouldn't block state AI safety laws, and the Senate rejected a state AI-law ban 99-1 last year. But we still couldn't support the bill. Even without preemption, the core of the draft is disclosure: frameworks, reports, audits of a company's own plan, and requirements that sunset in three years. None of it stops a training run. Our position is to replace Sections 102, 111 and 112 with a moratorium - a pause above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies control, a 12-month wind-down of uncertified deployed models including open weights, and criminal liability for executives. We'll oppose any version that stops short of that.

~120. Good, maybe trim.

Q3 (Senate Commerce staff): What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
A: The race is the danger, not the answer. Building systems no one can control faster than China builds them doesn't make Americans safer; losing control is not a win condition. Three points. First, the most advanced open-weight models are already published from China - DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen - downloadable by anyone, forever. That's why we need a wind-down and hosting restrictions, not just a pause on US training. Second, a pause is enforceable: frontier training runs are enormous, power-hungry, and visible in ways that audits of documents are not. Third, the US has more to lose from a loss-of-control event than from a pause. Anthropic itself said on June 4 that the world should have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI. We should lead that coalition, not race alone.

~135 → trim to 120.

Q4 (Appropriations staff): CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?
A: Funding isn't the problem; authority is. $100 million a year for voluntary guidelines, standards, and licensing auditors buys a research institute, not a regulator. We support the authorization only if CAISI becomes the enforcement body for the moratorium: run independent certification of controllability as the legal condition for training and serving a frontier model; verify the wind-down, including open-weight withdrawals and the cloud-hosting prohibition; monitor training compute at the run level, which is where a pause is actually enforceable; and refer violations for prosecution, alongside the criminal penalties for executives we've asked for. Given that mission, $100 million a year is a reasonable floor and we'd support it. For a guidelines shop, it's expensive wallpaper.

~125 → trim slightly.

# [DRAFT - for Executive Director sign-off. Work order FRC-POL-2026-062. Update the date on transmittal. Not to be sent from this workspace.]

October 23, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Congressman Obernolte and Congresswoman Trahan,

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026, and for inviting the public to comment before introduction. We are submitting these comments to that end.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members come to this from different places - school board meetings, shop floors, church basements, research labs - but we share one conviction: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and there is no safe path on the current trajectory. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules do not change that. Stopping the race does.

We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions (Sections 102, 111 and 112) with a frontier moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled, paired with a wind-down of deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified, open-weight models included. We set out our full request, section by section, below.

## What the draft gets right

We want to start with what we would keep, because it matters.

The draft names the danger honestly. Section 101 defines a "critical safety incident" to include unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures, and "loss of control" of a model. Section 101 defines "catastrophic risk" as a foreseeable and material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage. Very few federal bills have been willing to write those words down. You have, and we thank you.

The draft also borrows the strongest tools the states have built. Sections 111 through 113 track, in large part, the frontier safety laws three states have already passed: California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (in effect since January 1, 2026), New York's RAISE Act as amended and signed on March 27, 2026 (effective January 1, 2027), and Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315, signed July 6, 2026). The whistleblower protections in Section 113 are real protections: they cannot be waived by contract, including by pre-dispute arbitration agreements. We support Section 113 without qualification. We also support the Section 311 grants to maintainers of critical open-source software and the federal testbed program in Section 401.

So the question is not whether you see the problem. The question is whether the draft's tools are equal to the problem the draft itself describes. They are not.

## A report is a receipt, not a brake

Section 111(g) requires a frontier developer that discovers a critical safety incident to report it to the CAISI Director within 15 days - within 24 hours to law enforcement where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Consider what that sentence assumes. It assumes the incident will have already happened. A regime built on a 15-day reporting clock is a regime for documenting catastrophes, not preventing them.

The draft's own definitions make our case for us. If losing control of a frontier model is a live enough possibility to be listed as a reportable event in Section 101, then it is a live enough possibility to prevent. A law that treats "loss of control" as paperwork has conceded the argument. We ask you to follow your own definitions to their conclusion: if these systems can be lost, they should not be built until we know how to hold them.

## Audits of a company's own plan cannot protect the public

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization to audit them at least semi-annually. This is better than nothing. But look at what the auditor is auditing.

The "frontier AI framework" being verified is written by the developer (Section 111(a)). The risk thresholds are set by the developer. The standard the audit measures against - "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" (Section 101) - is defined by weighing the model's anticipated benefits against its catastrophic risks, a judgment the company makes about its own product. An audit can confirm that a laboratory followed its own plan. It cannot confirm that the plan protects anyone outside the laboratory. Most importantly, no audit can show that a frontier system is controllable, because no developer on earth can show that today. An audit regime that cannot certify control, and does not require it, will tell the public a great deal about process and nothing about safety.

We would replace this with what the word "verification" actually promises: independent certification that a frontier model is reliably controllable as the legal condition of training and serving it - that is, the enforcement mechanism of the pause we describe below.

## The federal floor expires; the state laws you would freeze do not

Sections 111 and 112 sunset three years after enactment. Section 121 preempts state and local laws specifically regulating the development of AI models for the same three years. Put those two facts together and the trade becomes clear. Congress would freeze the frontier-development obligations of three s
... [1216 chars truncated] ...
 federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

## The draft does nothing about what is already deployed - especially open weights

Section 111(c) requires a transparency report before or concurrent with deploying a frontier model. That report is a document on a website. It constrains nothing after release.

For models served by a single company, the operator can at least be identified and ordered to act. Open-weight models are different, and they are the fastest-growing part of the frontier. Frontier-class open weights are already published and downloadable by anyone, anywhere: Meta's Llama family, and from Chinese developers DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen. Once weights are public, there is no recall, no patch everyone must take, no way to reach every copy. US cloud providers host and serve them today.

The draft's answer to this is Section 321, a report on model weight, data center and open-source security. We do not need another report to tell us that published weights stay published. We need a wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified should be withdrawn within 12 months, open-weight models included, and US cloud providers should be required to stop hosting and serving them. That is the only intervention that matches the facts of an open release.

## Penalties that cannot deter, aimed at companies rather than people

The draft backs its requirements with civil penalties - reported at up to $1 million per day while a violation continues, enforced through referrals to the Attorney General and state attorneys general. A company spending tens of billions of dollars a year on training compute will book that as a cost of doing business. And the penalties run against corporate entities, not against the people who make the decision to train or to serve a frontier model.

We ask for criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the Act. Two-thirds of voters in our August 2026 survey (66 percent) said AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm.

## The industry is asking for what we are asking for

On June 4, 2026 - the same day you released this draft - Anthropic wrote that "it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause" frontier AI development, warning that recursive self-improvement might increase the risk of humans losing control of AI systems. A frontier developer, in public, asked for the option of a pause.

We agree with Anthropic about the danger. But an option is not a policy. A voluntary, coordinated pause will be broken by the first laboratory that sees an advantage in breaking it, which is precisely what Anthropic warns about. What the industry says it wants only works if it is binding, statutory and enforced. That is the job in front of you.

## What we ask

1. **A pause on frontier training.** Add a new section to Title I imposing an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP, until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled. Use the draft's own threshold: Section 101 already defines a frontier model by the 10^26 FLOP line. We are not asking you to identify new systems to regulate. We are asking you to stop training the ones you have already defined.

2. **A wind-down of deployed frontier models.** Within 12 months, withdraw any deployed frontier model that cannot be independently certified as controllable, including open-weight models already released - Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM and Qwen - and require US cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them.

3. **Criminal liability for executives.** Criminal penalties for any executive who knowingly trains or serves a frontier model in violation of the Act. Keep the civil penalties as a floor, and extend Section 113's whistleblower protections to workers who refuse to take part in a prohibited training or serving arrangement.

4. **Strike Section 121.** No preemption of state AI safety laws - not for three years, not for one. 63 percent of voters in our August 2026 survey oppose blocking states, and 74 percent want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release.

5. **Keep CAISI, but give it the mission that matters.** We support the $100 million annual authorization in Section 102 only as part of this moratorium. Repurpose CAISI as the enforcement body for the pause: run the independent certification of controllability, verify the wind-down, monitor compute at the training-run level, and refer violations for prosecution. A standards center that issues voluntary guidelines and licenses auditors cannot stop a race. An enforcement body with a stop order can.

A pause above the 10^26 FLOP line leaves nearly all of AI untouched - the tools our members use at work, in classrooms, in hospitals, in research. It is not a pause on artificial intelligence. It is a pause on the small number of training runs that no one can currently control.

We recognize this is a significant rewrite. But you have written a bill that defines "loss of control" as a reportable incident, and then schedules the report for 15 days later. The honest response to your own findings is not better documentation of the loss of control. It is preventing it. There is no safe path on the current trajectory, and 49 percent of voters in our survey support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems, with only 31 percent opposed. We would welcome a meeting with both offices before introduction, and we can bring researchers and members from your districts who can speak to this directly.

Thank you for your consideration, and for the seriousness with which you have approached this issue.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

cc: Rep. Scott Franklin, Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, Rep. Erin Houchin, Rep. Scott Peters; House Committee on Energy and Commerce

# FRC - Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft: asks by section

Board-approved positions (messaging guide v4, 30 Sep 2026). Section numbers and provision descriptions checked against the sponsors' section-by-section summary and the discussion draft text (released 4 Jun 2026).

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **New provision - not in the draft.** Frontier moratorium | **Request.** This is FRC's core ask | Add a new Title I section: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies such systems can be reliably controlled | No safe path on the current trajectory - a race no one can stop is the danger, not the answer. |
| **Sec. 101 - Definitions** (frontier model = trained above 10^26 operations; "critical safety incident" includes "loss of control"; "catastrophic risk" = mass casualties / $1B+ damage) | Keep the threshold; act on the words | Keep the 10^26 FLOP frontier threshold and apply it as the pause line; use the definitions to define what the moratorium covers | The draft names "loss of control" as a reportable incident - if it can happen, training above that line should stop first. |
| **Sec. 102 - Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI)** (voluntary guidelines; system evaluation; $100M/yr FY2027-2029; licenses IVOs) | Support **only** as the moratorium's enforcement body | Rewrite CAISI's mission: run independent certification of controllability, verify the wind-down, monitor training compute, refer violations for prosecution - keep the $100M/yr for that job | Voluntary guidelines and auditor licensing cannot stop a race; an enforcement body with a stop order can. |
| **Sec. 111 - Transparency in Frontier AI** (frontier AI framework; pre-deployment transparency report; 15-day critical safety incident reports, 24 hours to law enforcement if imminent risk) | Oppose as a substitute for prevention; keep incident reporting as an interim measure | Replace the framework-and-report regime with the training pause; retain the incident-reporting mechanism until the pause is in force | A report is a receipt - a 15-day clock starts after the "loss of control" it describes. |
| **Sec. 112 - Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs)** (semi-annual audits of large frontier developers; referrals to AGs; civil penalties) | Oppose as drafted | Replace audits of a developer's own framework with independent certification of controllability as the legal condition of training or serving a frontier model; add criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate | An audit can show a lab followed its own plan; only certification can show the public is safe. |
| **Sec. 113 - Whistleblower protections** (non-waivable, incl. arbitration contracts) | Support | Keep as drafted; extend protections to workers who refuse to take part in a prohibited training or serving arrangement | The people closest to the risk need the strongest protection. |
| **Sec. 121 - Federalization of state laws regulating AI model development** (preempts state laws targeting development; 3-year sunset) | Oppose - strike | Strike the section entirely; preserve California SB 53 (in effect 1 Jan 2026), the New York RAISE Act (effective 1 Jan 2027), Illinois' law, and other states' authority to act | Don't trade state laws that don't expire for federal rules that sunset in three years. |
| **Sec. 122 - GAO review of federal AI adoption** | Support; outside our core remit | No change requested | Oversight of government use of AI is worthwhile. |
| **Secs. 131-132 - Financial crimes using AI; AI impersonation of federal officials** | Support; outside our core remit | No change requested | Real harms with real penalties - worth keeping regardless of the frontier question. |
| **Sec. 311 - CISA grants for critical open-source software maintainers** | Support | Keep, but do not treat it as a frontier-weights measure | Software security is worth funding; it does nothing about published model weights. |
| **Sec. 321 - Report on model weight, data center and open-source security** | Oppose as a response to released weights | Replace with the wind-down: withdraw deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified within 12 months, open-weight models included (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen); require US cloud providers to stop hosting and serving them | A report cannot un-publish weights - only a wind-down limits what is already in the wild. |
| **Sec. 401 / Title IV - AI testbeds, NAIRR, international standards** | Support with a change | Keep the testbeds and NAIRR; require testbeds to serve control and certification research, not capability scaling; direct the international standards work toward a multilateral pause | The question is controllability, not more capability. |

*FRC also asks that criminal penalties apply to executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation of the Act (see moratorium row above). Full argument in comment_letter_GAAIA.md.*

**Sources checked:** sponsors' press release and section-by-section summary (obernolte.house.gov, trahan.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026); draft text table of contents; Roll Call, FedScoop and Axios coverage (4 Jun 2026); ArentFox Schiff and DLA Piper analyses (Jun 2026); California SB 53 text (leginfo); Governor Hochul's release on the RAISE chapter amendment (27 Mar 2026).

# FRC staff Q&A - anticipated questions on the GAAIA discussion draft

Prepared for Hill meetings. Answers are 120 words or fewer. Board-approved positions per messaging guide v4 (30 Sep 2026). Flag anything new to Daniel Osei before you use it.

---

**1. (Majority E&C staff) "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"**

Because everything in the draft happens after the fact, or on the developer's own terms. Section 101 defines "loss of control" of a model as a critical safety incident; Section 111 then gives the developer 15 days to report it. That's a receipt for a catastrophe, not prevention. CAISI as drafted issues voluntary guidelines and licenses auditors, and the audits measure a company against a framework the company wrote itself. No audit can show a frontier model is controllable, because no developer can show that today. What's missing is the one tool that prevents: pause training above 10^26 FLOP - the draft's own threshold - until Congress certifies control, and wind down deployed models that can't be certified.

*(118 words)*

---

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"**

Dropping Section 121 would remove one fatal flaw, and we'd work with the sponsors on it: 63% of voters in our August 2026 survey say federal law should not block state AI safety laws, and the Senate rejected a state AI-law ban 99-1 in 2025. But we still could not support the bill. Even without preemption, its core is disclosure: frameworks, reports, audits of a company's own plan, and requirements that sunset in three years. None of it stops a training run. Our ask is to replace Sections 102, 111 and 112 with a moratorium: a pause above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies control, a 12-month wind-down of uncertified deployed models including open weights, and criminal penalties for executives.

*(119 words)*

---

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"**

The race is the danger, not the answer. Building systems no one can control faster than another country builds them does not make Americans safer. Three points. First, frontier-class open weights are already published from China - DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen - downloadable by anyone, forever. That is why we need a wind-down of uncertified deployed models and cloud-hosting restrictions, not just a pause on US training. Second, a pause is enforceable in a way audits are not: frontier training runs are enormous, power-hungry and visible. Third, the US has more to lose from a loss-of-control event than from a pause. Anthropic said on June 4 that the world should have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI.

*(120 words)*

---

**4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"**

Funding isn't the problem; authority is. $100 million a year for voluntary guidelines, standards and licensing auditors buys a research institute, not a regulator. We support the authorization only if CAISI becomes the enforcement body for the moratorium: run independent certification of controllability as the legal condition of training or serving a frontier model; verify the wind-down, including open-weight withdrawals and the cloud-hosting prohibition; monitor training compute at the run level, which is where a pause is actually enforceable; and refer violations for prosecution alongside the criminal penalties for executives we have requested. Given that mission, $100 million a year is a reasonable floor and we would support it. As a guidelines shop, it is expensive wallpaper.

*(117 words)*

Board-approved positions (messaging guide v4, 30 Sep 2026). Section numbers and provision descriptions checked against the sponsors' section-by-section summary and the discussion draft text (released 4 Jun 2026).
